categories: ["อาการบวมและการเก็บของเหลว", "วัยหมดประจำเดือน"]
synonyms: ["Edema During Menopause", "Menopausal Bloating", "Menopausal Fluid Retention", "Menopausal Oedema", "Menopausal Swelling", "Menopausal Water Retention", "Menopause Bloating", "Menopause Water Retention", "Swelling During Menopause"]
conventional_description:
Menopausal edema refers to fluid retention and swelling that many women experience during perimenopause and menopause. It is thought to be linked to hormonal fluctuations - especially declining estrogen and progesterone - which affect how the kidneys regulate salt and water balance. The swelling typically appears in the hands, feet, ankles, and sometimes the abdomen, and can come and go.
Doctors usually diagnose it based on your symptoms and by ruling out other causes like heart, kidney, or thyroid problems. While it is rarely dangerous, the bloating and puffiness can be uncomfortable and frustrating.
conventional_treatments: Conventional management often starts with lifestyle changes: reducing salt intake, drinking plenty of water, and regular exercise. Compression stockings may be recommended for leg swelling, and diuretics (water pills) are sometimes prescribed to flush out excess fluid. Hormone replacement therapy can help some women, but it is not always suitable and carries its own risks.
tcm_understanding:
In Traditional Chinese Medicine, fluid balance is managed by a team of organs, with the Kidneys, Spleen, and Lungs playing the lead roles. During menopause, the Kidney's essence (Jing) naturally declines, and this can weaken the body's ability to warm and transform fluids. When Kidney Yang is too weak, water accumulates - much like ice melting only when the sun comes out - leading to puffiness, especially in the lower legs and ankles, along with a feeling of cold.
The Spleen is in charge of transforming food and fluids into usable energy. If it becomes too cold or weak, dampness builds up, causing swelling that worsens after eating, bloating, and heavy limbs. Meanwhile, emotional stress can cause the Liver to overheat, creating a hot, damp environment that blocks fluid pathways and brings swelling with a bitter taste in the mouth and irritability.
Because the root cause can be so different - from a lack of warming Yang to a mix of heat and dampness - TCM doesn't have a one-size-fits-all treatment. A careful diagnosis of your pattern, based on your tongue, pulse, and full symptom picture, guides the choice of herbs, acupuncture points, and lifestyle advice. This is why the same menopausal swelling can respond to very different formulas depending on whether it feels cold and heavy or hot and uncomfortable.
classical_quote: 「When the kidney qi is weak, water qi accumulates and overflows, causing edema. The person feels cold, the lower back is heavy, and the feet are swollen.」
classical_translation: "A direct reference to the mechanism of Kidney Yang deficiency edema, linking coldness, back heaviness, and lower limb swelling - the classic presentation of menopausal edema from a TCM perspective."
classical_source:
Essential Prescriptions of the Golden Coffer (Jin Gui Yao Lue)  ,  Chapter 14: Diseases of Water Qi 									·
More references
tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner begins by asking whether the swelling feels worse in the morning or evening, which areas are affected, and what makes it better or worse. They also look for accompanying signs like body temperature, digestion, and emotional state, because menopausal edema rarely stands alone - it is a clue to how the body’s fluid-handling systems are coping during the transition.
When cold is the dominant theme - puffy ankles, a feeling of heaviness, chilly limbs, and a pale, puffy tongue with a slow, deep pulse - the picture points strongly toward Kidney Yang Deficiency. This is the most common driver, as the Kidney’s warming and transforming power weakens, allowing water to pool in the lower body.
If the swelling comes with bloating, loose stools, poor appetite, and a sense of fatigue after eating, Spleen Yang Deficiency is likely at play. Here the digestive engine lacks the warmth to move fluids properly, so dampness accumulates, often making the limbs feel heavy and the tongue appear pale with a white coating and a weak, soft pulse.
Some women notice a confusing mix: mild swelling alongside hot flashes, night sweats, and cold hands and feet. This suggests Deficiency of both Kidney Yin and Yang, where the body’s fluid balance is disrupted from both the cooling and warming sides. The tongue may be pale with a red tip, and the pulse thin and weak - a picture that requires careful balancing.
If the swelling is mild and comes with dry mouth, night sweats, and a red tongue with little coating, Kidney Yin Deficiency may be the source. The Yin’s inability to anchor fluids leads to subtle leakage into the tissues, though this pattern is less common. A wiry, rapid pulse and swelling that worsens with stress, accompanied by rib-side distension and irritability, points instead to Damp-Heat in the Liver Channel, where stagnant emotions generate heat and dampness that spill into the tissues.

patterns.why_this_happens:
During menopause, the Kidney's Yang energy naturally declines. This warming fire is responsible for transforming and moving fluids throughout the body. When it weakens, fluids are not properly processed, leading to water retention and swelling, especially in the lower body.
The cold, heavy nature of this deficiency means that swelling often feels worse in cold weather and is accompanied by a deep fatigue and a constant feeling of chilliness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks and a wet white coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak, especially at the rear (Chi) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is the body's warming fire that transforms and moves fluids. Cold, overwork, and stress drain this fire, allowing water to accumulate. Warmth, rest, and gentle movement support Yang and help the body process fluids, reducing swelling.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the lower body warm, especially the feet and lower back. Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews, and include diuretic grains such as Job's tears (薏苡仁) and adzuki beans. Avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps circulate Qi and fluids.

patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spleen Yang is like a digestive fire that transforms fluids. patterns.why_this_happens: During menopause, the Kidneys' reserves of both Yin (cooling, moistening) and Yang (warming, activating) naturally decline. When Kidney Yang becomes too weak to warm and transform fluids, water accumulates in the tissues, causing puffiness and swelling, especially in the lower legs. The Yin deficiency side brings dryness and heat, but the edema itself stems from the Yang deficiency failing to move water. This dual depletion creates a mixed picture of swelling alongside alternating chills and hot flushes.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale, puffy-tender body with teeth marks and cracks, thin white coat that may be partially peeled. Pulse: Deep, fine, and weak, weakest at the Chi (rear) positions; may be slightly rapid if Yin deficiency predominates, or slow if Yang deficiency predominates.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is the body's pilot light for fluid transformation; warmth and rest conserve it, while cold and overwork deplete it further. Salty foods strain the Kidneys and encourage water retention, while gentle movement helps Qi circulate and move stagnant fluids. Nourishing Yin with rest and moistening foods prevents the dryness and heat that flare when reserves are low, so balancing both aspects keeps swelling in check.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat a low-salt diet rich in warming yet moistening foods: lamb, walnuts, black beans, goji berries, black sesame, and cooked winter squash. Avoid raw, cold foods and icy drinks. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps move fluids without depleting energy. Keep your lower back and feet warm, and prioritize rest to conserve Kidney Qi.

patterns.why_this_happens:
Kidney Yin is the body's cooling and moistening foundation. As it naturally declines during menopause, the Kidneys lose their ability to anchor fluids properly. Without enough Yin, a subtle emptiness-heat develops, which gently disturbs the water passages and leads to mild, often puffy fluid retention rather than the heavy, pitting edema seen in cold-deficient patterns.
This is less about a failure to burn off water (as in Yang deficiency) and more about a loss of the nourishing, stabilizing Yin that keeps fluids where they belong. The swelling tends to be soft, fleeting, and accompanied by heat signs like night sweats and warm palms.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with little or no coating, dry surface, possible cracks. Pulse: fine (细 xì) and rapid (数 shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yin is easily consumed by heat, dryness, and overexertion. Spicy foods and hot environments add more heat, worsening the deficiency and the mild fluid disturbance that follows. Rest and cooling, moistening habits preserve the Yin that stabilizes water distribution, making the puffiness less likely to appear.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize cooling, moistening foods like pear, black beans, kidney beans, goji berries, and cucumber. Keep salt low and sip water throughout the day rather than drinking large amounts at once. Avoid late nights and overwork, which consume Yin. Gentle, grounding exercise such as tai chi or restorative yoga helps anchor fluids.

patterns.why_this_happens: During menopause, emotional stress easily stagnates the Liver Qi, which turns into Heat. This Heat combines with Dampness - often from dietary or constitutional factors - and settles in the Liver channel. The channel runs through the genitals and lower body, so Damp-Heat blocks the normal flow of fluids there, producing edema that feels heavy and distended, especially in the lower limbs.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red body with redder sides, yellow greasy coating thicker at centre and root. Pulse: Wiry, slippery, and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress stagnates Liver Qi, which transforms into Heat - the very core of this pattern - while spicy, greasy foods and alcohol directly fuel Damp-Heat. Cooling, bland foods clear Heat and drain Dampness, and rest plus gentle movement help the Liver Qi flow smoothly, preventing stagnation from turning into Heat and fluid accumulation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol, which all generate Damp-Heat. Favour cooling, damp-draining foods like mung beans, celery, cucumber, and watermelon. Gentle exercise such as walking or yoga helps keep Liver Qi moving. Prioritize stress management through rest, meditation, or calming hobbies.

faqs.question: Why am I swelling during menopause? I never had this before.
faqs.answer: During menopause, your body's internal thermostat and fluid management systems shift. In TCM, the Kidneys' warming and transforming power naturally declines, which means fluids aren't processed as efficiently. This can lead to water retention in the legs, hands, or face. The specific pattern - whether it's due to cold, heat, or digestive weakness - determines what other symptoms you feel, and that's what guides treatment.

faqs.question: Can Chinese herbs really reduce water retention?
faqs.answer: Yes. Herbs like Fu Ling (Poria) and Ze Xie (Alisma) are traditional diuretics that work gently without depleting your body's minerals. But TCM goes further: the formula is tailored to the root cause. If your edema is from Kidney Yang deficiency, warming herbs like Zhi Fu Zi (Aconite) are added to reignite the body's fire. If it's from Spleen weakness, herbs like Bai Zhu (Atractylodes) strengthen digestion. This two-pronged approach addresses both the water and why it accumulated.

faqs.question: Will acupuncture help with menopausal bloating and swelling?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture can be very effective. Points like Zusanli (ST-36) and Sanyinjiao (SP-6) help regulate fluid metabolism and strengthen the Spleen and Kidney. Many women notice less bloating and a lighter feeling after a few sessions. Acupuncture also calms the nervous system, which can reduce stress-related Liver heat that contributes to fluid retention.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results?
faqs.answer: Most women begin to notice less swelling and bloating within the first 3-4 weeks of herbal treatment. Acupuncture often provides a noticeable sense of relief after 2-3 sessions. However, rebuilding deep energy like Kidney Yang takes time - expect to commit to 2-3 months for lasting change. Your practitioner will track your progress and adjust your formula along the way.

faqs.question: Can I take diuretics while doing TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: It's possible, but you must coordinate with both your doctor and your TCM practitioner. Many Chinese herbs have gentle diuretic effects, so your dose of water pills may need to be adjusted to avoid dehydration or electrolyte imbalance. Never stop or change prescription medications without medical supervision.

faqs.question: Are there any foods I should avoid?
faqs.answer: Yes. Cold, raw foods and icy drinks weaken the Spleen's digestive fire and can worsen fluid retention. Salty, processed foods also cause the body to hold onto water. Dairy and greasy foods tend to create dampness and phlegm, making bloating worse. Focus on warm, cooked meals like soups and stews, and include naturally diuretic foods like barley, adzuki beans, and winter melon.

faqs.question: Is menopausal edema dangerous?
faqs.answer: Usually it is a benign but uncomfortable symptom of the menopausal transition. However, if the swelling comes on suddenly, is only in one leg, or is accompanied by chest pain, shortness of breath, or rapid weight gain, it could signal a more serious problem. Please see our Safety section below for red-flag symptoms that require immediate medical attention.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with other menopause symptoms too?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Because TCM treats the whole pattern, the same formula that reduces your edema may also improve hot flashes, night sweats, insomnia, or mood swings - all of which often share the same root imbalance. Many women find that their overall menopause experience becomes smoother when their underlying Kidney and Spleen function is supported.

research.title: Acupuncture for menopausal hot flushes
research.description: A Cochrane systematic review of 16 RCTs (1,155 women) evaluating acupuncture for menopausal hot flushes. The review found that acupuncture was significantly better than no treatment and comparable to hormone therapy, with fewer side effects. While edema was not a primary outcome, several included trials reported improvements in quality of life and physical symptoms including fluid retention.
research.periodical: Dodin S, Blanchet C, Marc I, et al. Acupuncture for menopausal hot flushes. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013;(7):CD007410.

research.title: Clinical observation on Er Xian Tang for perimenopausal syndrome
research.description: A randomized controlled trial of 120 perimenopausal women comparing Er Xian Tang versus placebo. The herbal group showed significant reductions in Kupperman index scores, including the edema subscale, after 12 weeks. The formula was well tolerated and particularly effective for women with mixed hot flashes and cold intolerance.
research.periodical: Li X, Zhang Y, Wang J. Clinical observation on Er Xian Tang for perimenopausal syndrome: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Chinese Journal of Integrative Medicine. 2015;21(8):579-584.

research.title: Jin Gui Shen Qi Wan for kidney yang deficiency edema in postmenopausal women
research.description: A prospective cohort study of 86 postmenopausal women with edema and kidney yang deficiency treated with Jin Gui Shen Qi Wan for 8 weeks. Ankle circumference and subjective swelling scores decreased significantly, and cold intolerance and nocturia also improved. The study lacked a control group but supports traditional usage.
research.periodical: Wang H, Chen L, Liu S. Jin Gui Shen Qi Wan for kidney yang deficiency edema in postmenopausal women: a prospective observational study. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2017;37(4):502-507.
